INTRODUCTIONM
As you have seen, the telephone system is a communication system and uses many types of circuits.
Power supplies, amplifiers, oscillators, modulators, demodulators, multiplexers, and demultiplexers are just a few examples.
And, the circuits used for any one particular system depends on the system you choose to use.
To study all the types of circuits would require covering all aspects of electronics plus signal processing, communications, microwaves, fiberoptics, antennas, and transmission lines.
Not very practical. However, there is one circuit that is common to all telephone systems.
Let's begin the lesson on TELEPHONE EQUIPMENT.............................
LESSON MENU
DISCUSSION
The telset, it is the device you use every day.............
And, even though there are hundreds of different types, all telsets can be broken down into two general categories.
Although the mechanical telset has become somewhat of a novelty item, it is still useful for understanding basic telset operation. We will
A typical mechanical telset consists of a base unit and a hand set.
The base unit plugs into the telephone jack and has the ringer circuit, dialer network, voice network, and hook switch.
The hand set contains the input and output transducers (microphone and speaker) and is connected to the base unit by way of a spiral cord.
Even though newer mechanical telsets have the base unit and hand set combined, the operation is the same. Let's see.
The two wire local loop (green and red wires) connects into the base unit where the first circuit encountered is the ringer circuit.
The ringer circuit is a series resonant LC circuit. The inductors are bell solenoids while the capacitor blocks DC power.
With both L1 and L2 in the circuit, a 20 Hz AC signal produces resonance which operate the bell solenoids - your phone rings.
On some phones, a switch located on the bottom of the base unit allows you to short out one of the inductors reducing the volume of the ringer.
In this case, the resonate frequency is 30 Hz. Remember, the ring signal is a 20 and 30 Hz, 60 to 80 Volt AC signal.
Just past the ringer circuit is the hook switch, S1........
The switch has three parts, S1A, S1B, and S1C.
S1A and S1B make or break the series local loop.
When the hand set is on the base unit, the hook switch is pushed and opens, breaking the local loop.
Picking up the hand set causes the hook switch to close making the local loop, request for service.
S1C shorts out the speaker when the local loop is open to prevent "clicks" when the hook switch is activated.
Which component in the telset is a bell solenoid?
TRY AGAIN!
C1 is a capacitor that blocks the DC power to the telset from the ringer circuit.
S1 is the hook switch that is used to make or break the local loop.
The next circuit is the dialer network.....................
Switch S2A is mechanically connected to the dialer and sequentially opens and closes as the dialer rotates - on the return rotation.
S2A opens and closes a specific number of times to produce pulses for each digit dialed.
For example, dialing a 5 followed by a 3 produces a set of five and three pulses as shown.
Circuits located in the End Office count the pulses to determine the number dialed.
Switch S2B is used to short the speaker while dialing to prevent you from hearing the pulses.
C2, R1, and R2 act as an automatic volume control.
C2 couples voice signals to R2. R2 is a varistor that inversely changes its resistance according to the level of the applied voltage.
If the signal level on the local loop increases, the resistance of R2 decreases, allowing more of the signal to be shorted around the voice network.
If the signal level on the local loop decreases, the resistance of R2 increases, allowing less of the signal to be shorted around the voice network.
The last circuit is the voice network that separates the outgoing voice signal from the incoming voice signal.
Recall that the transmitted and received voice signals are both on the local loop. This is called "duplex transmission".
The outgoing voice signal from the microphone is coupled to T2A.
By transformer action, the voice signal is passed to T2B and placed on the local loop.
The voice signal is also passed to T1B and T1C. However, the signal in T1 is out of phase, as indicated by the dots, and cancel.
This prevents the transmitted voice signal from reaching the speaker.
C3, C4, and R3 are used to exactly balance T1 and T2 for proper operation.
However, most people prefer to hear a small amount of their own voice in the speaker.
So, R3 is adjusted so a small amount of the transmitted signal is not canceled in T1 and reaches the speaker -- this is called sidetone.
The received voice signal from the local loop is applied to T1B and T2B in series.
This in turn sets up in phase signals in T1C and out of phase signals in T2C.
Consequently, the received signal is induced in T1A and passed on to the speaker.
While the received signal is cancelled in T2A and blocked from the microphone.
In the dialer network, what is the purpose of C2, R1, and R2?
TRY AGAIN!
The voice network of T1 and T2 separate signals on the local loop.

TRY AGAIN!
R1 is part of the automatic volume control but does not change resistance. R1 is not a varistor.
R3 is part of the voice network that separates the incoming signal from the outgoing signal. It is not a varistor, it is a variable resistor.

TRY AGAIN!
If the signal to the speaker is in phase to the transmitted signal, the speaker would pick up the outgoing voice signal.
TRY AGAIN!
R3 is adjusted to slightly mismatch T1 and T2 so a small amount of the transmitted signal reaches the speaker, not adjusted so most of the transmitted signal does not reach the speaker....
Now, let's look at the electronic telset...................
A typical electronic telset consists of a base unit and a hand set, just like the mechanical telset.
Again, newer electronic telsets have the base unit and hand set combined, but the operation is the same.
The major difference between a mechanical telset and an electronic telset is the dialer and the circuits inside the base unit.
The electronic circuits are what give you the added features such as memory dialing, speed dialing, etc.
These electronic circuits also allow for cordless operation of the phone. Cordless phones use FM signal processing between the hand set and base unit.
The electronic circuits used are IC chips. One IC can be used as the ringer circuit, voice network and dialer network.
For simplicity, let's look at a discrete block diagram of a typical electronic telset.
With the hand set on the base unit, on hook, S1A and S1B are open as shown.
R1 presents a high resistance to voice signals and C1 blocks any DC current.
However, the ring signal will be passed by R1 and C1. D2 and D4 rectify the AC ring signal (20 and 30 Hz 60 - 80 VAC) to pulsating DC.
S1B then routes the pulsating DC through D6 and D7, zener diode limiter and clipper, and activates the electronic ringer circuit -- your phone rings.
When you pick up the hand set, off hook, S1A and S1B close...
S1A closing shorts out R1 and C1 allowing the small level voice signals and DC power to reach the circuits in the telset through closed S1B.
D1 through D4 ensures that the DC power applied to the line voltage regulator is the correct polarity.
This prevents damaging the telset IC chips if the green and red wires are mistakenly reversed.
Normally, the green wire is positive and the red wire is negative. D2 and D3 are forward biased routing positive polarity power to the line voltage regulator.
If the wires are reversed, D1 and D4 are forward biased routing positive polarity power to the line voltage regulator.
From S1B, the +DC voltage is routed to the line voltage regulator, D5 limits the DC voltage applied.
The regulator produces the power to operate the rest of the circuits in the telset.
The voice network separates the incoming and outgoing voice signals.
The outgoing signals are routed from the microphone through the voice network to the local loop. D1 through D4 allow the complete voice signal to pass.
The incoming signals are routed from the local loop through the voice network to the microphone. D1 through D4 allow the complete voice signal to pass.
Also, the Dual Tone Multiple Frequency (DTMF) dialer inputs tones to the voice network which are placed on the local loop.
The crystal produces the fundamental frequency that is used to generate the different tones for each number dialed.

Now, let's look at example circuits used in the voice and dialer networks.

The voice network uses a differential amplifier, normally an op-amp configured for a differential amplifier. Recall that a different amplifier rejects common mode signals and operates similarly to the transformer circuit in the mechanical telset.
The outgoing voice signal from the microphone is applied to the base of Q1, to the base of Q2 through Q3, and to the local loop.
Since Q3 is a common collector, emitter follower, the signal applied to Q2 is the same level and in phase with the signal applied to Q1.
Since Q3 is a common collector, emitter follower, the signal applied to Q2 is the same level and in phase with the signal applied to Q1.
DEFINITION
COMMON COLLECTOR/EMITTER FOLLOWER - The common collector/emitter follower amplifier has a unity voltage gain (gain of 1) and no phase inversion.
With the speaker connected across the collectors of Q1/Q2 and with Q1/Q2 amplifying the same signal, there is no difference in potential across the speaker.

The speaker does not respond to outgoing voice signals. The variable resistor in the collector of Q2 circuit is adjusted to balance the conduction of Q1 and Q2 and is offset a little to produce sidetone.

The incoming voice signal from the local loop is only applied to Q2. The signal is isolated from Q1 by Q3 which also isolates the signal from the microphone. With only one input applied, the collector of Q1 remains constant and the collector of Q2 varies. This sets up a potential difference across the speaker and produces an output.....
Consequently, there is a difference in potential across the speaker and the speaker responds.
The dialer network uses a key decoder, two frequency dividers and a crystal.
Pressing a button sets up two inputs to the key decoder, one for the row (R) and one for the column (c), a matrix.
The key decoder then sends a signal to the high and low tone dividers that selects tones depending on the number dialed.
The high frequency of the crystal, 3.579545 MHz, is used to produce accurate tones when divided.
The two frequencies or tones produced depends on the number dialed or which button was pushed (values are in Hz).
Newer electronic telsets use additional buttons for added functions.

Now let's look at the experiment card circuitry using a functional block approach.
The PC130-338 card has four functional processes: INTERFACE, CONVERSION, SWITCHING and POWER GENERATION.
The interface function is accomplished around the boundaries of the card. Any signal that penetrates the boundary must interface with the card via a physical connection.
Interface connections include 15v power (from the trainer), phone jacks, and fiber links. The fiber links have dual functionality, interface and conversion.

Conversion is a change process. In the case of the fiber optic ports, designated Tx (gray) and Rx (blue), this is from electrical to light (Tx) and light to electrical (Rx). The output is converted again by the amplifiers...

The amplifiers boost and/or combine the signals. The most significant conversion process is local loop (duplex) to Tx/Rx (simplex), then back to local loop. The summing amplifiers add local loop and the receive signal (Rx) from the other circuit...

Switching is accomplished manually on the PC130-338 card. This is a critical network function. In LL (Local Loop) position, the switch connects the local loops in series. In LD (Long Distance) position, the local loops are connected to the toll office circuitry (amplifiers and fiber interface)...

Power Generation starts functioning when the 15v source is applied. Integrated circuits produce -5v and +5v to run the electronics on the card. The local loops use the straight 15v inputs to run the talk battery circuit in the voice network...
